relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: A prophet's widow cries out because debt is reaching for her children.
Elisha begins with what remains in her house, however small.
Neighbors' empty vessels become the shape of communal capacity.
Behind a shut door, mother and children participate in survival.
The children bring, the mother pours, and scarcity stretches.
The oil stops only when there is no more vessel.
Debt is paid, and the family lives on what remains.
A great woman of Shunem insists on feeding the passing prophet.
She discerns holiness through repeated presence.
She creates a room with bed, table, chair, and lamp.
The prophet rests in the space she made.
She is called and stands before the prophet's household.
She refuses court access and says she dwells among her own people.
Her lack of a son becomes the issue named by Gehazi.
She stands in the doorway, boundary and threshold together.
The promise of a son frightens her because false hope wounds.
The child is born at the promised season.
The child grows and goes to the harvest field.
His head pain sends him back to his mother.
He dies on her knees at noon.
She lays him on the prophet's bed and shuts the door.
She moves quickly toward the man whose promise altered her life.
Her shalom is not denial but disciplined motion under crisis.
She refuses delay on the road.
Elisha sees her coming from Carmel's distance.
She answers shalom even while grief is driving her.
She grasps the prophet's feet, and gatekeeping is stopped.
Her protest exposes the wound: I did not ask to be deceived with a son.
The staff is sent ahead with urgent instructions.
The mother refuses to leave Elisha, as Elisha once refused to leave Elijah.
The staff alone does not awaken the boy.
Elisha enters the room where death is lying.
The door closes and prayer begins.
Body meets body in a strange act seeking warmth and life.
The child sneezes seven times and opens his eyes.
The mother is called to lift up her son.
She receives him and leaves with life restored.
Famine turns the prophetic company toward a shared pot.
Unknown gourds enter the stew because hunger gathers whatever can be found.
The meal becomes danger: death in the pot.
Flour marks the pot for eating again.
Firstfruits arrive as barley loaves for the hungry.
The servant counts scarcity; the word speaks enough.
They eat, and there is leftover.

contemplative_note: 2 Kings 4 is a food-and-body chapter: oil against debt slavery, a room for rest, a mother's protest after child death, a poisoned pot made safe, and barley shared beyond calculation. The miracle current runs through material care, not spectacle.
